passage: Ten minutes before the school's recitation contest, Aparna, ten, sat with her poem in her village language, Bhojpuri, trembling in her hands. Two weeks ago some classmates had laughed at her accent and said, "Say it again, it sounds so funny." Since then Aparna had spoken only textbook Hindi and had stopped singing to herself. Her teacher, Ms. Rehana, saw the paper. "Is that the poem your grandmother taught you?" Aparna nodded. "Then read it. I want the whole school to hear it." Aparna's voice shook at first. By the last line the hall was silent, and then the clapping was loud. Ms. Rehana told her, "Speaking two languages is a gift many of us wish we had."

qa.a: Aparna's poem was in her village language, Bhojpuri.

qa.q: Which choice by Ms. Rehana protected Aparna's pride?
qa.a: Ms. Rehana asked about the poem, told Aparna to read it and said the school should hear it, praising the skill of speaking two languages.

qa.a: Possibly surprised and a little embarrassed. The applause showed them that the accent and language deserve respect.

Madhuri, ten, moved from a village near Ballia to a school in Pune. On the first day, when she answered in class, her Bhojpuri accent made two boys giggle. One copied her: "Hum ka kari?"
After that, Madhuri stopped raising her hand. At home she told her mother, "Don't speak Bhojpuri when you pick me up."
The class teacher, Pradeep Sir, noticed. In the next class, he asked the children how many languages they could speak. Most said two. Madhuri whispered, "Four. Bhojpuri, Hindi, a bit of Marathi, English."
Pradeep Sir said, "Four! That's the most in this class. Madhuri, teach us a Bhojpuri song on Friday?"
The boys who giggled went quiet. On Friday, Madhuri sang.

qa.q: How many languages did Madhuri say she could speak?
qa.a: Madhuri whispered, "Four. Bhojpuri, Hindi, a bit of Marathi, English."

qa.q: Why did Madhuri ask her mother not to speak Bhojpuri?
qa.a: Madhuri felt ashamed and embarrassed after the boys mocked her accent, so she wanted to hide her mother tongue.

qa.q: What did Pradeep Sir do that protected Madhuri's pride?
qa.a: He praised her four languages as a skill and invited her to teach a Bhojpuri song, which turned her accent into something to be proud of.

qa.q: How might the boys see Madhuri after Pradeep Sir's words?
qa.a: They may feel embarrassed about mocking her and start to see her as skilled rather than strange.

grounding: A child mocked for a village accent starts hiding her mother tongue, and a teacher who praises her multilingual skill protects her pride.

First week. Lalremsiami, nine, joined a school in Delhi. When she spoke Mizo to her mother at the gate, some children laughed and copied the sounds in a mocking sing-song. The next day, she told her mother, "Speak Hindi only. Or English."
Second week. Her teacher, Damini Ma'am, heard about it. She asked Lalremsiami quietly if she'd teach her how to say "thank you" in Mizo. "Ka lawm e," Lalremsiami whispered. Damini Ma'am practised it all day, badly, making her smile.
Fourth week. In assembly, Damini Ma'am asked Lalremsiami to say "good morning" in Mizo to the whole school. Lalremsiami's hands shook. But she did it. Hundreds of children repeated it. Walking home, she spoke to her mother in Mizo, loudly, all the way.

qa.q: How do you say "thank you" in Mizo, according to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Lalremsiami whispered, "Ka lawm e."

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel when she asked her mother to speak only Hindi or English?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and hurt after the children laughed at her language.

qa.q: What made Damini Ma'am's approach work?
qa.a: She showed genuine interest in Mizo, learned a word herself, then gave Lalremsiami a proud public moment, protecting both the child and her language.

qa.q: What would change if Damini Ma'am had done nothing?
qa.a: Lalremsiami might keep hiding Mizo, and the language could slowly fade from her life.

grounding: Over several weeks, a child mocked for her mother tongue starts hiding it, and a teacher who values it restores her pride.

Anand, you're laughing at your cousin's Kannada accent? Come here. Let me tell you something.
When I was eight, my family moved from our village near Udupi to Mumbai. My Hindi was stiff and my Marathi was nothing. At home we spoke Tulu. The first time I said a Tulu word in class, the whole room laughed. After that I refused to speak Tulu, even to my own grandmother. She'd call me, and I'd answer in Hindi. I saw her face fall every time.
Then my teacher, Mr. Kamath, heard me mutter a Tulu word by mistake. He said loudly, "You speak Tulu? That's a treasure. Almost nobody here can." He asked me to write a Tulu poem for the school magazine.
I spoke to my grandmother in Tulu that evening. She cried.
So, Anand, stop laughing. This is your Madhav Ajja telling you: every language is a treasure.

qa.q: Where did Madhav's family move from?
qa.a: They moved from their village near Udupi to Mumbai.

qa.q: How did Madhav's grandmother feel when he answered her in Hindi?
qa.a: She felt hurt and sad; her face fell every time he refused to speak Tulu.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Madhav's story?
qa.a: Mr. Kamath praised his Tulu as a treasure and asked him to write a poem, which helped him take pride in his language again.

qa.q: How did Madhav's grandmother react when he spoke Tulu again?
qa.a: She cried, likely from relief and joy at hearing her grandson speak their language again.

grounding: An elder recalls being mocked for his mother tongue as a child and hiding it, until a teacher's praise restored his pride.
